analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits and pays for it by taxing high incomes.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on June 29, 2026 and referred to three House committees, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would increase Social Security checks across the board, raise the minimum benefit for people who worked many years at low wages, use a cost-of-living formula that better reflects what seniors actually buy, end the five-month wait for disability benefits, credit caregivers with Social Security earnings, extend benefits to student children up to age 26, and rebuild Social Security's staffing and field offices [S2]. To pay for it, the bill would remove the cap on wages subject to the Social Security payroll tax and apply that same 12.4% tax to investment income above $400,000 a year [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security and disability beneficiaries — especially low-wage workers, people with long careers, widows and widowers in two-income households, family caregivers, disabled applicants, and children in grandparent-headed households. Every beneficiary gets the across-the-board increase, and the minimum benefit is set at the poverty line for long-term low earners [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the 90% benefit formula factor with 93%, an across-the-board increase in monthly checks for 2027 through 2036 [S2].
Sets a new minimum benefit tied to the federal poverty guideline for workers with at least 11 years of work, rising with each additional year up to 30 years [S2].
Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to whichever index is higher — the standard wage-earner CPI or a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers [S2].
Eliminates the five-month waiting period before disability benefits begin [S2].
Credits up to five years of unpaid care for children or chronically dependent relatives as deemed wages worth about half the national average wage [S2].
Extends child's benefits to full-time post-secondary students up to age 26 and eases benefit access for children living with grandparents or other relatives [S2].

Raises benefits for widows and widowers in two-income households, adds a 5%-per-year benefit bump after 15 years on the rolls, and stops benefits from being clawed back when a wage-index change would otherwise cut them [S2].
Directs rebuilding of the Social Security customer service workforce, keeping field offices open, and protecting beneficiaries' data [S2].

Funds these changes by repealing the wage cap on the Social Security payroll tax after 2026 and adding a 12.4% Social Security tax on net investment income above a $400,000 threshold, on top of the existing 3.8% Medicare investment tax [S2].

analysis.who_pays: High earners and owners of investment income. Once the wage cap is repealed, wages above the current cap (about $184,500 in 2026) become subject to the full 12.4% payroll tax split between workers and employers, and investment income above $400,000 becomes subject to the same tax [S2]. Self-employed high earners pay the full share themselves [S2].

drawbacks.text: Repealing the payroll-tax cap and adding the 12.4% tax to investment income above $400,000 is a large, permanent tax increase on high-income households and on capital income; critics argue taxing investment income through a payroll-style levy discourages saving and investment [S2].

The benefit improvements in the bill text are scheduled to apply for calendar years 2027 through 2036, with many provisions explicitly expiring after 2036 — so the boost is temporary on its face rather than a permanent benefit increase [S2].
Employers bear half of the newly uncapped payroll tax on high salaries, a cost businesses with highly paid workforces would push back on [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is broad and targets the people most dependent on Social Security: the lowest earners, the disabled, caregivers, and the very old. The cost is concentrated on a small slice of high earners and investors, who would see significant new taxes. The main design weakness is that the bill's own text sunsets the benefit increases after 2036, which leaves the '2100' promise dependent on a future Congress extending them. On balance, the gains for ordinary beneficiaries far outweigh the costs, which fall almost entirely on the top of the income distribution.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to three House committees — Ways and Means, Education and Workforce, and Energy and Commerce — and nothing has happened since; no hearing, no vote, and Congress is still in session [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. John Larson introduced the Social Security 2100 Act in the House on June 29, 2026 [S1].

The Speaker referred it to the Ways and Means Committee, and in addition to Education and Workforce and Energy and Commerce, a multi-committee referral that splits the bill's provisions among three panels [S4].
As of the latest action record, no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled on the bill [S4].
The bill has 3 cosponsors, all Democrats, joining the Democratic sponsor [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet in a final sense, but the outcome so far favors the status quo: high earners and investors keep the current tax structure, and House Republicans, who control which bills get committee time and floor votes, have not moved it. Social Security beneficiaries get none of the proposed increases.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and the House majority

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Social Security 2100 Act on June 29, 2026 and has long championed this benefit-expansion-and-tax framework [S1][S4].

for.name: Three Democratic House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsors [S3].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 29, 2026 and has taken no action on it since — no hearing or markup appears in the action history [S4].

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Controls the House floor agenda in the 119th Congress
against.what_they_did: Controls which bills reach the floor; no floor action has been scheduled on this bill [S1][S4].

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors are Democrats; with Republicans holding the House majority and no Republican cosponsors, the bill has purely Democratic support so far [S3].

industries.note: The bill would subject their wages above the payroll-tax cap and their investment income above $400,000 to the 12.4% Social Security tax [S2]. Their financial interest in the bill's fate runs directly against the benefit increases ordinary beneficiaries would receive, since the new taxes are the bill's funding source.
With the wage cap repealed, employers would owe the 6.2% employer share of the payroll tax on every dollar of high salaries, not just wages up to the cap [S2].
Self-employment income would lose its cap under SECA, so high-earning sole proprietors and contractors would pay the full 12.4% on all net earnings above $400 [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican House majority, only Democratic cosponsors, and a split across three committees, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or a vote this Congress. Its realistic path is as a messaging vehicle: it may gain more cosponsors and inform the next round of Social Security negotiations, but it will most likely expire at the end of the 119th Congress without floor action unless its provisions are attached to a broader package.
